newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh seeks to revive privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh seeks to revive privatisation.

text.p: Bangladesh, vowing to speed up its privatisation programme, has begun selling government shares in public limited companies, the chief of the Bangladesh Privatisation Board (PB) said on Wednesday.
"Majority shares in nine companies are currently being offloaded in the stock exchanges," Kazi Zafarullah told members of the Foreign Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
He said revenue from the sales would be about 100 million taka ($2.3 million) during the 1996/97 fiscal year ending June 30.
Zafarullah, himself a private entrepreneur, was chosen by the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina as privatisation board chairman to restore vigour to the disinvestment process.
Bangladesh has divested only 12 state-owned enterprises (SOE) since the country adopted denationalisation as a policy about 12 years ago.
Zafarullah said he had listed 61 units for immediate privatisation.
PB officials said tenders had been floated in the past fortnight for selling 25 SOEs, while a further five would be offered on Thursday.
Zafarullah said the board was being strengthened to include members of parliament, labour leaders and professionals.
He said the board had been given permission to sell on its own authority small units valued up to 100 million taka.
"I am also trying to frame a legal framework for privatisation and cutting down red tape. I can assure you that there is now a strong political will in favour of privatisation," he said.

Earlier during a meeting with the Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Zafarullah said the country had suffered nearly $1.86 billion in losses over five years due to inefficient public enterprises.

He called the loss-making public enterprises -- which were overstaffed and mismanaged -- a "cancer of the economy" that cost the government 25 billion taka ($580 million) each year, or an equivalent of two percent of gross domestic product.

"We have no option but to go for aggressive privatisation. The slow and uneasy process of privatisation has caused a total loss amounting to some 80 billion taka (nearly $1.86 billion) from fiscal 1991-92 to 1995-96 (July-June)," Zafarullah said.
He said the government had given 420 billion taka ($9.76 billion) in subsidies to SOEs over the past 21 years.
"The SOEs were also given huge loans, but 90 percent of it, nearly 130 billion taka ($3.02 bln), has not been repaid," Zafarullah said.
"This has resulted in a severe liquidity crisis in the lending banks."
Ailing industrial units should have been swiftly transferred to private ownership to prune their management, inject fresh capital and create jobs, he said.
He also said the privatisation programme faced stiff opposition from restive labour unions and political groups, helping to delay the process.
